displayQuote: None are so old as those who have outlived enthusiasm

meta.title: Who really said "None are so old as those who have outlived enthusiasm"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Thoreau everywhere, but the line traces only to an 1886 anthology and isn't found in his own writings. An honest look at an apocryphal favorite.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'None are so old as those who have outlived enthusiasm'?
meta.ogDescription: Pinned on Thoreau by every quote site, yet unsourced in his works and first surfaced in Kate Sanborn's 1886 anthology. Attributed, not verified.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Thoreau on virtually every quote site, and the sentiment fits his lifelong faith in wakefulness and enthusiasm. But no one has located these exact words in his books, essays, letters, or journal. The earliest known appearance is a posthumous anthology — Kate Sanborn’s A Year of Sunshine (1886) — where it is already just handed to “Thoreau” with no citation. Treat it as attributed, not verified.

source.heading: The paper trail
source.excerpt: None are so old as those who have outlived enthusiasm.
trail: The quote is absent from the sourced, disputed, and misattributed sections of the Wikiquote Thoreau page, and Quote Investigator has never run an entry on it — unusual for a genuine, locatable Thoreau line.

The sourcing site WIST marks it “(Attributed)” and notes it was “first attributed in Kate Sanborn, A Year of Sunshine; Cheerful Extracts for Every Day in the Year (1886), but not found in his writings.”
Popular databases such as Goodreads reproduce it with the name attached but no work, edition, or page — the hallmark of a free-floating attribution.
source.excerptNote: Presented on quote sites as a standalone aphorism. No fuller passage in Thoreau’s writing has ever been produced to surround it, which is itself a warning sign for a line credited to so voluminous a journal-keeper.

sourceLink.text: WIST sourcing note for the Thoreau attribution

source.rightsNote: Whichever way it falls, the text is in the U.S. public domain: if the line is genuinely Thoreau’s it predates his 1862 death, and its earliest documented appearance — Kate Sanborn’s A Year of Sunshine (1886) — is likewise long pre-1931. No living rights-holder attaches to the wording.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: About Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American essayist, poet, and naturalist, best known for Walden (1854), his account of two years of deliberate, simplified living at Walden Pond, and for the essay Civil Disobedience (1849). A central figure of New England Transcendentalism alongside his mentor Ralph Waldo Emerson, he kept a vast Journal that runs to millions of words. His aphoristic, quotable style has made him one of the most heavily — and most loosely — quoted writers in American history.

misattribution.heading: Why the Thoreau credit is shaky
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “famous-name magnet” quote: an uplifting aphorism pinned to a beloved author with no source ever attached. The attribution may even be old, but old is not the same as verified.

items.why: Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes and countless graphics credit Thoreau but cite no work; the line does not appear in Walden, Civil Disobedience, his essays, letters, or the published Journal as indexed by Wikiquote.

Per WIST, the first known instance is in Kate Sanborn’s A Year of Sunshine (1886), a day-by-day book of “cheerful extracts” published 24 years after Thoreau died — exactly the kind of Victorian compilation that circulated names faster than sources.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: it is credibly and widely attributed to Thoreau, but no primary source has ever been produced, and its earliest trace is an 1886 anthology rather than anything in Thoreau’s own hand — so we mark it attributed, not verified, following WIST.

context.heading: A sentiment that outran its source
lead: Thoreau really did prize enthusiasm and “wakefulness” — it is one of the animating ideas of Walden — which is precisely why a line like this attaches to him so easily and stays attached. The thought sounds like him, so readers stop checking whether the words are his.

The result is a quote that is genuinely useful and genuinely well-loved, and also genuinely unsourced. It sits in the honest gray zone between ‘he said it’ and ‘he didn’t’: credited for well over a century, but never once tied to a page.
context.pull: Old is not the same as verified.
